Beyond Core: Azure Cosmos DB's Multi-Model Power

Leveraging diverse APIs for specialized data needs and seamless integration.

What is Multi-Model?

Azure Cosmos DB supports multiple data models (document, key-value, graph, column-family) through various APIs. This means it can act as a compatible endpoint for different NoSQL databases, allowing you to choose the best fit for your data structure and application needs.

Why it Matters for Architects

  • Migration Ease: Lift-and-shift existing NoSQL applications without major code rewrites.
  • Developer Familiarity: Use existing SDKs and query languages (e.g., MongoDB drivers).
  • Global Scale: Inherit Cosmos DB's global distribution and high availability.
  • Guaranteed Performance: Benefit from Cosmos DB's SLAs and Request Unit (RU) model.
Key Takeaway

Cosmos DB's multi-model design allows it to emulate popular NoSQL APIs, enabling developers to use familiar tools and data models while benefiting from Azure's globally distributed, high-performance backend.

Module 6›Chapter 6.5›MongoDB API
API Deep Dive

Integrating with MongoDB Applications

Seamless migration and development with the Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB API.

Core Functionality

The MongoDB API provides a wire-compatible endpoint for MongoDB, allowing applications to interact with Cosmos DB using standard MongoDB client drivers and SDKs. This means your application perceives Cosmos DB as a native MongoDB database.

Key Use Cases

  • Lift-and-shift: Migrating existing MongoDB applications to Azure.
  • New Applications: Building new solutions within the MongoDB ecosystem.
  • Flexible Document Storage: When MongoDB's query language and features are preferred.
Key Takeaway

The MongoDB API enables easy migration of existing MongoDB applications and supports new development within the MongoDB ecosystem, leveraging Cosmos DB's managed service benefits.

Benefits & Considerations

Benefits

  • Familiarity for MongoDB developers.
  • Access to MongoDB's rich query language.
  • Seamless integration with existing tools.

Considerations

  • Minor differences/unsupported features vs. native MongoDB.
  • Performance/cost still governed by Cosmos DB RUs and partitioning.

Example Scenario

A gaming company uses MongoDB for user profiles and game state. To achieve global reach and reduce operational overhead, they migrate their database to Azure Cosmos DB using the MongoDB API. Their existing Node.js backend code requires minimal changes, primarily updating the connection string, allowing them to quickly scale globally.

Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Cassandra API
API Deep Dive

Scaling with Cassandra Workloads

Migrating high-throughput, write-intensive applications with the Cassandra API.

Core Functionality

The Cassandra API offers a wire-compatible endpoint for Apache Cassandra, allowing existing Cassandra applications to connect and interact with Cosmos DB using their familiar drivers and Cassandra Query Language (CQL).

Key Use Cases

  • Migration: Lift-and-shift existing Apache Cassandra applications to Azure.
  • High-Throughput: Ideal for write-intensive applications requiring linear scalability.
  • Time-Series/IoT: Well-suited for storing large volumes of time-series or IoT sensor data.
Key Takeaway

The Cassandra API enables seamless migration of Apache Cassandra workloads to a fully managed, globally distributed service, ideal for high-throughput, write-intensive applications like IoT and time-series data.

Benefits & Considerations

Benefits

  • Zero-code change migration for many Cassandra apps.
  • Fully managed service, no cluster management.
  • Global distribution with guaranteed SLAs.

Considerations

  • Requires careful Cassandra data modeling (partition/clustering keys).
  • Understanding CQL and its limitations is necessary.
  • Not suitable for complex joins or ad-hoc queries.

Example Scenario

An energy company collects vast amounts of sensor data from smart grids, currently stored in an on-premises Apache Cassandra cluster. To reduce infrastructure costs and improve data ingestion latency globally, they migrate to Azure Cosmos DB's Cassandra API. This allows them to continue using their existing data model and CQL queries while offloading cluster management to Azure.

Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Gremlin API Intro
API Deep Dive

Modeling Connected Data with Gremlin

Understanding vertices, edges, and graph database fundamentals for the Gremlin API.

Graph Data Fundamentals

Graph databases represent data as a network of interconnected entities. The Gremlin API implements Apache TinkerPop's Gremlin query language, a powerful tool for traversing these complex networks.

Vertices: The Entities

  • Represent individual data points or entities.
  • Can have properties (key-value pairs) describing them.
  • Examples: User, Product, Location, Order.

Edges: The Relationships

  • Represent connections or relationships between vertices.
  • Can also have properties describing the relationship.
  • Examples: 'knows' (between users), 'buys' (user to product), 'located_in' (product to location).

Visualizing Graph Data

Key Takeaway

The Gremlin API models data as vertices (entities) and edges (relationships), using the Gremlin query language to efficiently traverse and analyze highly connected data structures.

Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Shared Foundations
Core Concepts

Shared Foundations: RUs, Distribution, and Consistency

Understanding common infrastructure concepts across all Cosmos DB APIs.

Request Units (RUs)

  • Definition: The fundamental currency for throughput in Cosmos DB.
  • Impact: Every database operation (read, write, query) consumes RUs, regardless of the API.
  • Importance: Critical for managing performance and cost; optimization is key.

Global Distribution

  • Capability: Replicate data across multiple Azure regions with a single click.
  • Benefits: Low-latency access for users worldwide, robust disaster recovery.
  • Availability: A core feature accessible to all Cosmos DB APIs.
Key Takeaway

All Cosmos DB APIs share the same underlying infrastructure, meaning concepts like Request Units (RUs), global distribution, and consistency models are universal, despite differing data models and query languages.

Consistency Models

Five Models

Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual. Choose based on your application's needs for data freshness and availability.

Universal Application

These models apply to data accessed through any Cosmos DB API, allowing architects to define the desired consistency level for their entire database account.

Analogy: The Global Library

Imagine Cosmos DB as a global library. Each API is a different way to organize and access books (data) – some use a card catalog (SQL), others a digital index (MongoDB), or a relationship map (Gremlin). But all these methods rely on the same library building (global distribution), the same librarians (RUs for operations), and the same rules for how quickly new books are available everywhere (consistency models). The underlying infrastructure is unified, even if the access method differs.
